Let's look at this from a logical perspective.
If you ask the person "will any of your minions successfully bleed x this
turn". According to you, the can only answer yes or no.

If they answer yes, that means they must bleed X this turn, ie they have to do
everything they can to bleed that person(stealth/using all your minions).
However _if_ X has enough intercepts and/or other reactions cards such as
telepathic counter, none of the bleeds will go through successfully, and
therefore the person has not fufilled his/her requirement to bleed X(and
furthermore cannot b/c he/she has used all his cards and minions).

Since there is an inherent flaw in answering yes(the possibilty that it will
not be fulfilled), the person being asked the question must therefore answer
"no" or risk lying.

Hence, if you were a really devious person, you could ask each person "will
you successfully oust anyone from this game any time during this game" and
because of the above arguement, they have to answer "no" because its the only
answer that they will be able to follow through on. Therefore you can win the
game by asking each of your opponents that question because following that,
they must refrain from ever ousting anyone.

Obviously this is not the way the monocle is to be used(otherwise the entire
game is FUBARed). Perhaps an official ruling on what one is allowed to ask
with the monocle?

Answering no is the right thing to do in this case, and would only mean

opportunity to do so. What you are asking is "for all minions, for all
situations when that minion is untapped and ready, will it attempt to
bleed?"

attempt to hunt (or equip, or call a vote). Since I can do this anytime
before the game ends, this question isn't much of a constraint.

not bleed, then you must also agree that a "yes" answer is satisfied by one
minion bleeding once.)

Actually, after thinking about this question for a bit I've realized
something. Namely, that the interpretation of the question is irrelevant.
What matters is whether you contradict your answer or not.

Let's take a trip down memory lane and have a hypothetic meth. ask his hyp.
prey "Whenever you have ready untapped minions during the game will you
attempt to bleed your prey?".

Now everyone agrees that if he says yes, that he has to bleed whenever he has
ready untapped minions(or at least thats what it seems to be)

Now the disagreement comes when said prey says "no".
People think that if the askee says "no" that all he/she has to do is fulfill
the statement not(Whenever you have ready untapped minions during the game,
will you bleed your prey) [yes I used logic gates just to be more general and
unspecific). So in essence, if you say "no" you can fulfill that one
statement and then go on later to bleed your prey.

There is one big problem with that. If later on you have ready untapped
minions and you go bleed your prey, the you are contradiciting your answer to
"whenever you have ready untapped minions during the game, will you bleed your
prey?". Why do I say this? Simple. Before you can attempt to bleed your
prey, you have untapped minions right?

(space left for arguement over this point)

Therefore the first part of the question is true, you have ready untapped
minions. Now if you bleed your prey, the second part of the question is
also true(you have attempted to bleed your prey).

(space left for arguement over this point)

So in essence, you have bled your prey when you had untapped minions(which
requires a yes answer to the question).

(space left for arguement over this)

But before you said no to the question. You have contradicted your answer.
The main point I'm trying to make here is that the question is not whether you
fulfill what your interpretation of the question is or not. The question is
whether you've followed your answer to the monocle question or not.

Messages.Author: Michael B. Moore
Messages.Body:
In article <3ca3b6$t...@news.acns.nwu.edu> jo...@merle.acns.nwu.edu (Josh Hsu) writes:
>Let's take a trip down memory lane and have a hypothetic meth. ask his hyp.
>prey "Whenever you have ready untapped minions during the game will you
>attempt to bleed your prey?".
>

>Now the disagreement comes when said prey says "no".

Let's try again. "Whenever" means this turn and next turn and the next
until the end of the game. So let's look at a simpler question, "This turn
will you attempt to bleed your prey and next turn will you attempt to bleed
your prey?"

If I answer "no", then I have three choices. I can wait for two turns
before attempting to bleed my prey. I can bleed my prey this turn but not
next turn, or I can bleed my prey next turn but not this turn. The only
thing I am forbidden from doing by my "no" answer is trying to bleed my
prey both turns.

Suppose instead you ask a similar question about the next three turns. My
"no" answer leaves me several choices, the only choice forbidden to me is
three consecutive attempts to bleed. As long as one of those turns I do
not attempt to bleed my prey, I have acted in a way consistent with my
answer.

Your "whenever" question is asking about every turn until the end of the
game. As long as one of those turns I do not attempt to bleed my prey, I
have acted in a way consistent with my "no" answer.

================================================================

Asking "What will your answer to the monocle's next question?" is a
borderline yes/no question. What someone is really doing is naming the
word they will use, rather than answering a question affirmatively or
negatively.

================================================================

Precisely interpreting natural language is a large research area. For an
introduction to logic used in contemporary linguistics, you may be
interested in this book:

James D. McCawley, Everything that linguists have always wanted to know
about logic but were ashamed to ask. University of Chicago Press, 1981.

Mike Moore

Messages.Author: David Michael Kass
Messages.Body:
In article <3c69vu$8...@news.acns.nwu.edu>,

Josh Hsu <jo...@merle.acns.nwu.edu> wrote:
>Ok, so according to you guys, you only have to fulfill what you perceive to be
>the question.
>Thats find and dandy with me (I don't have a monocle =])

No, we're just using the rules of formal logic that naturally limit the power
of the monocle. I'll try to explain the key point we're using without
resorting to formalism (I apologize to all of you who know formal logic, but
you're the ones who already understand this). This is binary logic (ie there
are only two possible answers).

There are 4 possible cases that can result in complex questions (ones that
potentially involve more than one event/time): Always, Never, At least once,
At least not once. These cases come in pairs and whenever yes specifies one
of the pair, no specifies the other one. The pairs are: {Always and At least
not once} and {Never and At least once}. The question itself specifies which
pair the answer can come from (and which is yes and which is no in the pair).
Thus the person answering the question can always specifiy one of the two
At least once conditions, and keep the question from being very limiting.

For simple questions (involving only one event at one time) the two possible
pairs are identical. Always and At least once are the same (since there is
only one item); and Never and At least not once are also the same. Thus
they are probably more useful questions since they put more constraints
on the person answering the question.

All of these assume questions about the future, and what is a person required
to do to satisfy their answer.

To help clarify, here are a couple examples:
Will you bleed your prey whenever possible?
This is an Always / At least not once type question (whenever is the
key word here) and answering yes chooses Always where as no chooses At least
not once (and is the better choice).

Will you not block all my actions this turn?
This is an Never / At least once type question (not and all are the
important words here), again, no is probably the better choice since it
chooses at least once and only requires you to block one action, but allows
you to block more if desired. Especially since failing to block does not
tap the vampire.

>So lets take the case where my predator uses the monocle and asks me the
>question "Will you successfully bleed your prey during your next turn" and I
>answer no.

This is an At least once / Never (since never is the no answer). Thus
answering no means that you cannot attempt to bleed your prey (unless you can
guarantee that, no matter what anyone does, the bleed will not be successful--
the only way I know of to do this is bleed with a 0 bleed ally). Answering
yes forces you to bleed you prey at least once and keep on trying until the
bleed is successful (possibly trying with all vampires than are ready and
untapped).

The difficulty is in determining which pair a question refers to and which
is yes and which is no. A question that means the same thing (but with
different words) can actually use the other pair. For example
Will you allow all my actions to succeed? is effectively the same question
as my second example, but the answer is actually in the Always / At least
not one pair. In general, questions that other players can affect the
at least (not) one case will be more powerful since they may require the
player to use additional resources to fulfil the case. Also, the longer the
time interval (and/or the more attempts possible), the less restricting the
question. Thus the more you try to control with the question (ie all of the
rest of the game versus the next turn), the less restricting the other case
will be.

I hope this helps clarify the use of the Monocle...

Messages.Author: Michael Constant
Messages.Body:
The Men in Black <bre...@ptang.bevc.blacksburg.va.us> wrote:
> I do agree that one question from the Monnocle can't be as bad as others
>seem to think: faulty logic being used to eliminate more possibilities than
>a yes/no question realy can. However, a series of questions, if unrestricted,
>can be devestating IMOH.

Oh no, a single question from the Monocle can be devastating. Suppose
I ask you, "is it true that you will either answer no to this question
or never harm me for the rest of the game".

If you answer yes, then it's true that you either answered no to the
question or you'll never harm me (remember that you must answer truth-
fully). Since you didn't answer no to the question, then it must be
true that you'll never harm me. Cool.

If you answer no, then it's false that you either answered to to the
question or you'll never harm me. However, this is a logical contra-
diction, since you actually did answer no to the question, making the
correct answer yes! Therefore you can't legally answer no.

So the upshot is that when I ask you the question above, you must answer
yes, and therefore you must never harm me for the rest of the game.

In case you haven't figured it out already, this is insanely powerful.
I would therefore recommend that everyone play with the recommendation
issued by WotC: that the questions must pertain directly to the game.
This means that any questions which refer to themselves, other questions,
or someone's personal life (I really should try that one sometime :-))
are treated as illegal.

The Monocle is a cool card when you don't abuse it; let's not force WotC
to ban it or take it out of print.
--
Michael Constant (mco...@soda.csua.berkeley.edu)

Ah...but you're forgetting the true essence of Jyhad...Fine, I, the
Methusela won't hurt you for the rest of the game, but here comes Smudge and
he wants blood!

You may argue that doing this is not in the spirit of fairness, but then
again, is asking the original question very fair? Lying and mis-direction
is what this game is all about. A similar example is when using the Monocle
in conjunction with Game of Malkav:

Player A: If I play Game of Malkav this turn, will you hold 5 blood in your
hand?
Player B: Yes.

During Master phase, Player A plays Game of Malkav, and holds out 4 blood.
Player reveals the contents of his outstretched hand...it contains 3 blood.

Player A: You said you'd hold 5 blood in your hand! You can't do that!
Player B: Oh, but I can...

Player B brings his other hand from under the table and opens it, revealing
5 blood counters. He has been faithful to his answer, and Player A is now
down 4 blood.

As with the above example, more often than not, if your opponent tries to
screw you with the Monocle, you can screw him even more. It's like granting
a Wish spell in Dungeons & Dragons. The players may THINK that they've
worded their wish perfectly.....

Bottom line, a clever and deceitful player should not be able to avoid
getting burned by the Monocle. If your opponent insists on asking
unbalancing questions, you have every right to be an absolute stickler.
With power comes a price...

Just my 2 cents,

On using the monocle to ask questions about future monocle answers:

The monocle requires that you answer questions truthfully, and does
not permit you to "change you mind" later, you must stick to your answer if
possible. The monocle doesn't doesn't affect your future actions, it just
forces you to give accurate imformation about them. If you are asked
whether you will answer yes to the next question, you might answer 'no'. If
you are then asked 'Will any of your minions ever take an action again?', then
you have a dillema. Obviosly your minions are going to take actions again at
some point, and the monocle requires you to answer truthfully, so it is not
possible for you to answer no to this question, and you MUST answer yes,
despite your first monocle answer.

Of course this is all based on the assumption that the monocle can not
affect your future actions, but only reveal them. Any opinions?
Disagreements?

Larrx...

(This argument doesn't affect most other monocle questions, by the way. The
only reason it's 'not possible' is because the monocle itself demands true
answers. Will you bleed, block, do you have these cards, etc. questions are
still fine.)

Messages.Author: Jon Inge Teigland
Messages.Body:
The Monocle of Clarity says:

During your untap phase, if bearer is ready, you can ask any Methuselah

a yes or no question. He or she must answer truthfully. If the question

pertains to the future, he or she must abide by the answer if possible.

Using the Monocle is not an action.

So.
Q1: Will you answer 'yes' to the next question I ask with the monocles ?
A1: No.
Q2: Will you ever attempt to bleed me during the remainder of this game ?
A2: Yes.

Now you may say this is not legal, since I must abide by the answer if
possible, however, I WILL attempt to bleed you later in the game, so it
is not possible to abide by the answer. Now you may say I can choose not
to bleed you later in the game, and since the monocles say I must abide
by the answer if possible, then I must choose not to attempt to bleed you
later during the game. However, first I choose wether I will attempt to
bleed you later during the game, at this point I have not given an
answer to the second question, so I do not have to abide by that, also
my decision have nothing whatever to do with the first question, so I
don't have to care about that either. I choose to attempt to bleed you
later during the game. This is perfectly legal. Then I have to consider
the question you asked. Since I have decided to attempt to bleed you, I
have to answer yes to your question.

Wether this is legal may be discussed, but I think it is fair enough,
and it gives a good limitation on the monocles. At least that is
how I will use them if I am ever asked a question like this. That is,
unless I choose to hit the owner of the card hard in the head with
a chair, and then burn the card. For real.

Jon Inge Teigland

One point which is clearly stated on the card, but lots of people seem
to keep missing is that the Monacle is intended to allow you to force
someone to do something. I'll even go further and say that smart and
non-cheesy uses of it will force someone to do something they didn't want
to do (example later.) The "proof" of this is the card text. If you are
asked about a _future_ action, you have to pick and answer and abide by
it.

are trying to ignore this part of it. "Are you going to bleed me for
at least 1 pool next turn?" Your honest answer is more-than-likely
going to be "it depends," but the card is clear about what you have to
do. You are forced to pick either 'yes' or 'no' and then follow up on
it.
I didn't ask "Are you planning to bleed me next turn?" so you can
honestly answer 'no' and later change your mind after I do something.
The Monacle' clearly indicates it can be used to force someone to commit
to a future action.

suppose I have two minions, Bleeder and Fighter, and I ask you if you
will block my next action. You are going to try to block everything
Bleeder does, and will never block Fighter (you let him bleed you for
1 if he really wants to.) Unfortunately, you can't say that.
A 'yes' answer means you may be forced to use KRCG for +1 intercept
in order to block Fighter equiping with a second Machine Gun (and
get cut to ribbons by him.) A 'no' answer forces you to let Bleeder
suck 8 resource points from your pool.
This is a smart, non-cheesy and lethal use of the Monacle'.
